about: A shop 'Orrin & Vale' and a camera written KESSEL OPTIK, Kessel Optik and Kessels: one brand and one camera, so the halves 'Orrin' and 'Vale' and the variants 'KESSEL OPTIK' and 'Kessels' are not separate names.
title: The Corner Shop
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Arcade
paragraphs: Anneke bought her first camera from Orrin & Vale, the shop on the corner of the arcade. She paid in coins.
The camera was a KESSEL OPTIK, heavy as a brick, with a lens cap on a string. The label said so in capital letters.
Orrin & Vale sold everything a photographer could want. Anneke went there on the first of every month.
She wrote to the makers of the Kessel Optik about a stiff shutter. They replied within a week.
Anneke loaded a roll and walked down to the market. She photographed the fishmongers and the pigeons.
At Orrin & Vale the clerk shook his head over the shutter. He said the Kessel Optik had a famous weakness.
The Kessels, he added, were no longer made. Every Kessels he had ever sold had come back for repair.
Anneke asked what a Kessels cost second-hand. The clerk named a price that made her laugh.
She kept the camera anyway. Anneke liked the weight of the thing and the sound it made.
A new poster hung in the window of Orrin & Vale. KESSEL OPTIK, it said, in letters a foot high.
Anneke stopped to look at it on her way home. She thought the poster made a promise the camera could not keep.
Next month she took the Kessel Optik back to the shop. Orrin & Vale mended it for the price of a lunch.
The clerk showed her a smaller camera in a leather case. Anneke turned it over and handed it back.
She preferred her Kessels. She said it had character, and the clerk agreed that it did.
Anneke photographed the regatta in June. The Kessel Optik jammed twice and caught the winning boat.
The picture ran in the local paper. Orrin & Vale framed a copy and hung it by the till.
Anneke went in to thank them. The clerk said the credit belonged to the Kessels, and to the light.
In the district everyone knew Anneke, and nobody had a bad word for Anneke.
Years afterwards people still asked about Anneke, though few could say why.
